guides.title: Backyard Vegetable Garden Quick Start
guides.summary: Start small with reliable vegetables, simple beds, and water-conscious layouts so the garden becomes productive before you scale it up.
steps: Choose a sunny area that gets at least six hours of light and is close to a water source.
Start with a few dependable crops such as tomatoes, beans, lettuce, silverbeet, and herbs for your season.
Improve soil first with compost and mulch before adding more crop variety.
Expand only after one small bed is producing consistently.
guides.notes: Local season, heat, and water limits matter more than planting everything at once.

guides.title: Water-Efficient Gardening for Drought
guides.summary: In drought or hot summers, garden design matters more than enthusiasm. Mulch, timing, shade, and crop choice are the main levers.
steps: Water deeply and less often so roots move downward instead of staying shallow.
Mulch exposed soil heavily to slow evaporation and reduce temperature swings.
Group thirsty crops together and keep hardy crops in the hottest or driest edges.
Use temporary shade cloth during heatwaves and wind events.
guides.notes: Do not use scarce drinking water blindly. Match crop area to realistic stored water and rainfall.

guides.title: Native Edible Plants Basics
guides.summary: Native edible plants can be useful in Australian gardens, but only plant and consume species you can identify confidently and source safely.
steps: Start with a few well-documented edible natives suited to your state and climate.
Grow labelled plants from reputable nurseries instead of relying on wild identification alone.
Keep records of what is planted, when it fruits, and how it is prepared safely.
Treat any unfamiliar wild plant as inedible until confirmed by a trusted regional source.
guides.notes: Never guess on wild plant identification. Some native plants have inedible or toxic lookalikes.

guides.title: Composting and Seed Saving Basics
guides.summary: Compost builds resilience in the soil, while seed saving helps preserve crop continuity across disruptions and seasonal shortages.
steps: Keep a simple compost stream using kitchen scraps, dry carbon material, and regular turning.
Avoid diseased plant material and meat or dairy in small household compost systems.
Save seeds from healthy, open-pollinated plants once they are fully mature and dry.
Label and store saved seed in cool, dry, dark conditions.
guides.notes: Hybrid seeds may not grow true to type. Start with simple, reliable crops for saving.

guides.title: Urban Food Production in Small Spaces
guides.summary: Small balconies, courtyards, and rentals can still produce herbs, greens, and compact vegetables if container layout and watering are consistent.
steps: Use containers sized to the crop so roots do not dry out too quickly.
Grow fast-turnover foods first such as herbs, lettuce, spring onion, and compact tomatoes.
Stack production vertically with shelves, rails, or trellises where safe.
Check moisture daily because container gardens fail fastest through missed watering.
guides.notes: Container gardens can become water-hungry in wind and heat. Match plant numbers to what you can maintain.
